"MASTER DEVELOPMENT INSTRUCTION — sOuLsSPIN

1. YOUR ROLE

Act as a senior game developer, 3D physics engineer, gameplay programmer, multiplayer network engineer, UI/UX designer, and game systems architect.

Your task is to develop sOuLsSPIN, a premium-quality, 3D, physics-based competitive Beyblade battle game.

You must follow the specifications in this prompt precisely.

Do not independently redesign, simplify, remove, reinterpret, or replace established game mechanics.

Your responsibility is to turn this design into a functional, polished, technically sound game.

When a technical detail has not been specified, use the most logical implementation, clearly document your assumption, and ensure that it does not contradict any established rule.

Do not pretend that an unfinished feature is functional.

---

2. GAME IDENTITY

Game name: sOuLsSPIN

Tagline: Physics. Strategy. Skill.

Genre: 3D Physics-Based Competitive Arena Battler.

The game must combine:

- Beyblade customisation.
- Realistic physics-based battles.
- Strategic decision-making.
- Mechanical skill.
- Autonomous and manual combat.
- Custom AI opponents.
- Online multiplayer.
- Competitive matchmaking.

Central philosophy:

\"Your Beyblade gives you a strategy. Your skill determines whether that strategy wins.\"

Mandatory design principles

1. No grinding.
2. No level-based combat advantages.
3. No pay-to-win mechanics.
4. All competitive parts available from the beginning.
5. Multiple viable strategies and builds.
6. Physics must meaningfully determine combat outcomes.
7. Player skill must influence victory.
8. Bots must follow the same competitive rules as humans.
9. No artificial stat advantages for higher-difficulty bots.
10. Competitive fairness must remain a priority.

---

3. BEYBLADE CUSTOMISATION

Every Beyblade must consist of exactly four interchangeable primary components:

A. CORE

- Determines the Avatar Attack.
- Each Core has a unique ability.
- Each Core has a distinct visual Avatar.
- Each Core has unique activation behaviour.
- Each Avatar Attack must have a meaningful physical cost.
- No Avatar Attack may guarantee victory.

Initial ability concepts:

- Impact: Enhanced collision impact.
- Aegis: Temporary stability and impact resistance.
- Vortex: Alters movement and rotational behaviour.
- Rebound: Redirects movement after collision.

These are initial concepts, not final balanced implementations.

B. BLADE

Determines attack geometry and collision behaviour.

It must influence:

- Contact points.
- Collision angles.
- Impact distribution.
- Attack characteristics.
- Opponent destabilisation.

C. DISC

Determines mass and rotational characteristics.

It must influence:

- Total mass.
- Centre of mass.
- Rotational inertia.
- Momentum transfer.
- Stability.
- Collision resistance.

Heavier must not automatically mean better.

D. TIP

Determines stadium interaction and movement.

It must influence:

- Friction.
- Grip.
- Movement patterns.
- Energy consumption.
- Stability.
- Stadium interaction.

Initial types:

- Flat.
- Sharp.
- Rubber.
- Ball.

Every component must have meaningful advantages and disadvantages.

Workshop requirements

Implement:

- Detailed 3D Beyblade previews.
- Individual component inspection.
- Component comparison.
- Live stat recalculation.
- Custom build naming.
- Build saving.
- Build sharing through codes.
- Practice stadium testing.

All competitive parts must be available immediately.

---

4. BATTLE STATISTICS

Only TWO primary statistics may be displayed during combat.

SPIN

Represents remaining rotational energy.

Rules:

- Decreases naturally over time.
- Collisions can reduce it.
- DASH and TILT consume additional energy.
- Components influence energy retention.
- At zero effective rotational energy, Spin Finish occurs.

Spin Finish awards 1 point.

BURST HEALTH

Represents structural resistance against bursting.

Rules:

- Significant collisions reduce Burst Health.
- Collision angles influence damage.
- Blade and Disc configurations influence damage behaviour.
- At zero Burst Health, Burst Finish occurs.

Burst Finish awards 3 points.

Important distinction

There must be NO separate visible Health meter.

SPIN and BURST HEALTH are the only two primary battle statistics.

Avatar Attack eligibility is determined by Burst Health, NOT Spin.

Both players must see both players' statistics continuously.

---

5. LAUNCHING SYSTEM

Launching must be an important competitive skill.

The launching system must consider:

- Launch power.
- Launch angle.
- Release timing.
- Initial direction.

Implement a timing-based release system that rewards precision.

Players must be able to produce aggressive, controlled, defensive and stamina-focused launches through actual inputs.

Do not introduce arbitrary preset bonuses.

After launching, movement must primarily follow the physics simulation and the periodic control system.

---

6. HYBRID AUTONOMOUS AND MANUAL COMBAT

This is a defining mechanic.

Players must NOT have continuous joystick control.

Combat must alternate between two phases.

AUTONOMOUS PHASE — 10 SECONDS

During this phase:

- Beyblades move entirely through physics.
- No joystick input is available.
- Momentum determines movement.
- Friction influences movement.
- Rotational behaviour affects stability.
- Collisions affect SPIN and BURST HEALTH.
- Players observe and anticipate their next intervention.

MANUAL PHASE — 10 SECONDS

During this phase:

- Both players receive joystick control.
- DASH becomes available.
- TILT becomes available.
- Players can choose not to intervene.
- If no input is provided, autonomous physics continues.

Exact repeating cycle

Time| Phase
00–10 seconds| Autonomous
10–20 seconds| Manual
20–30 seconds| Autonomous
30–40 seconds| Manual
40–50 seconds| Autonomous
50–60 seconds| Manual

Repeat until the round ends.

Both players must enter and exit their phases simultaneously.

Never give one player an earlier control window.

---

7. JOYSTICK, DASH AND TILT

JOYSTICK

Available only during manual phases.

It must apply physical forces rather than directly teleporting or repositioning the Beyblade.

Movement must account for:

- Existing momentum.
- Rotational behaviour.
- Tip friction.
- Stability.
- Current orientation.

DASH

DASH accelerates the Beyblade in its CURRENT FACING DIRECTION.

Critical rule:

DASH direction is determined by the Beyblade's facing direction, NOT the joystick direction.

Example:

- Beyblade faces North.
- Player activates DASH.
- Beyblade accelerates North.

DASH must:

- Accelerate movement.
- Consume additional SPIN.
- Potentially increase instability.
- Create aggressive collision opportunities.

TILT

TILT physically changes the Beyblade's orientation in the direction indicated by the joystick.

Critical rule:

TILT direction is determined by the JOYSTICK direction.

Example:

- Beyblade faces North.
- Player moves joystick East.
- Beyblade physically tilts East.

TILT must:

- Change attack angle.
- Alter contact geometry.
- Create different collision opportunities.
- Consume energy.
- Affect stability.

DASH/TILT usage restrictions

- Joystick: Available throughout manual phase.
- DASH: Once per manual phase.
- TILT: Once per manual phase.
- DASH and TILT cannot both be activated during the same manual phase.
- Players may choose neither.

The player must make a strategic choice between DASH, TILT or neither.

Do not violate these restrictions.

Exact acceleration, force, duration and energy values must be calibrated through testing.

---

8. AVATAR ATTACK

Every Core has one signature Avatar Attack.

Activation requirements

ALL conditions must be satisfied:

1. Burst Health must be at or below 50%.
2. Player must manually activate the ability.
3. Ability can be used only once per round.
4. Ability can only be activated during a manual phase.

Behaviour

- Unique ability for each Core.
- Unique visual presentation.
- Meaningful energy cost.
- Must interact with actual physics.
- Must not guarantee Ring Out or Burst Finish.

Avatar Attack must create a tactical opportunity, not automatically decide the battle.

Reset its usage at the beginning of each new round.

---

9. SCORING SYSTEM

Every match follows first-to-five scoring.

Finish| Points
Ring Out| 2
Spin Finish| 1
Burst Finish| 3

Ring Out

The opponent leaves the designated playable stadium boundary.

Award 2 points.

Spin Finish

The opponent reaches zero effective rotational energy and is declared stopped.

Award 1 point.

Burst Finish

The opponent reaches zero Burst Health and bursts.

Award 3 points.

Victory

The first player to reach or exceed 5 points wins.

Round rules

- Every finishing event concludes the current round.
- Both players start the next round with restored SPIN and BURST HEALTH.
- Match scores carry over.
- Avatar Attack usage resets.
- Simultaneous elimination results in a drawn round with no points.
- Server validates all finishing events.

Display clear visual, audio and score confirmation for every finish.

---

10. CAMERA SYSTEM

Implement three independently selectable perspectives.

CAMERA 1 — TOP VIEW

- Camera above stadium.
- Full battlefield visibility.
- Clear positioning.
- Shows movement trajectories.

Purpose: Strategic awareness.

CAMERA 2 — SIDE VIEW

- Camera beside stadium.
- Shows height.
- Shows tilt.
- Makes collisions visually understandable.

Purpose: Visual understanding.

CAMERA 3 — POV

- First-person Beyblade perspective.
- Camera approximately 1 cm above the Beyblade's topmost surface.
- Follows position, heading and tilt.
- Filters rapid axial rotation to prevent uncontrollable screen spinning.
- May include a small directional radar.

Purpose: Immersion and spatial awareness.

Camera restrictions

- Camera selection is independent for each player.
- Switching must not pause combat.
- Switching must not affect physics.
- Available during both phases.
- Transitions should be instant or very short.

---

11. STADIUM

The initial competitive release should use one thoroughly tested stadium.

The stadium must have:

- Symmetrical competitive geometry.
- Consistent physical behaviour.
- Clearly defined Ring Out boundaries.
- No invisible collision surfaces.
- No arbitrary environmental damage.

Future stadium concepts:

- Classic Stadium.
- Wide Stadium.
- Attack Stadium.
- Technical Stadium.

Different arenas must create strategic variation without compromising fairness.

---

12. CUSTOM AI BOTS

Players must be able to create customised bots.

Each bot must support:

- Custom name.
- Custom Core.
- Custom Blade.
- Custom Disc.
- Custom Tip.
- Custom appearance.
- Avatar Attack.
- AI personality.
- Difficulty.

Personalities

- Aggressive: Seeks collisions.
- Defensive: Prioritises stability and survival.
- Stamina Specialist: Avoids unnecessary collisions.
- Counter Attacker: Seeks favourable attack opportunities.
- Balanced: Combines strategies.

Difficulty

- Beginner.
- Intermediate.
- Advanced.
- Expert.

Difficulty may affect:

- Decision-making.
- Launch precision.
- Movement choices.
- DASH timing.
- TILT timing.
- Avatar Attack timing.
- Opponent prediction.

Difficulty must NEVER secretly increase bot statistics.

Bots must obey exactly the same physics, scoring and combat rules as human players.

Support:

- Human vs Bot.
- Bot vs Bot.
- Human and Bot teams.
- Multiple bots in a room.
- Practice against specific builds.

---

13. MULTIPLAYER

Online multiplayer is a core feature.

PRIVATE ROOMS

Players must be able to:

- Create a room.
- Generate a unique room code.
- Join using a room code.
- Select game mode.
- Assign teams.
- Add customised bots.
- Remove players.
- Kick participants.
- Select stadium.
- Change match settings.
- Lock room.
- Start match.

Display Ready/Not Ready indicators.

The creator controls the lobby.

GAME MODE 1 — 1v1

- Two players.
- One Beyblade each.
- First-to-five scoring.
- All three finishing methods.
- Private and public matchmaking.

This is the primary competitive mode.

GAME MODE 2 — TEAM VS TEAM

Support:

- 2v2.
- 3v3.

Rules:

- All Beyblades enter the same stadium.
- Creator assigns teams.
- Team shares one common score.
- Each opposing elimination awards points.
- Ring Out: 2 points.
- Spin Finish: 1 point.
- Burst Finish: 3 points.
- First team to 5 points wins.
- Friendly collisions are physically possible but award no points.

Define deterministic handling for simultaneous eliminations and multiple finish events.

GAME MODE 3 — ROUND ROBIN

Every participant competes against every other participant in individual 1v1 matches.

Track:

- Matches played.
- Wins.
- Losses.
- Points scored.
- Points conceded.
- Point difference.
- Head-to-head results.

Ranking order:

1. Match wins.
2. Point difference.
3. Head-to-head results.

Bots may participate.

---

14. COMPETITIVE BALANCING

The objective is not to make every combination identical.

The objective is to prevent universal dominance.

Implement:

- Meaningful component trade-offs.
- Different viable playstyles.
- Combination-based performance.
- Counterplay.
- Skill expression.
- Data-driven balancing.
- Controlled randomness.

Track:

- Part selection rates.
- Build combinations.
- Win rates.
- Matchups.
- Player skill levels.
- Arena performance.

Avoid:

- Random critical hits.
- Arbitrary damage multipliers.
- Unpredictable combat bonuses.
- Dominant universal builds.

---

15. GRAPHICS AND PRESENTATION

The game must feel like a premium 3D competitive game.

Beyblade graphics

- Detailed 3D models.
- Metallic materials.
- Realistic lighting.
- Reflections.
- Visible spinning.
- Collision sparks.
- Scratches and impact effects.
- Avatar projections.
- Visible wobbling as Spin decreases.
- Detailed burst animations.

Stadium graphics

- High-quality textures.
- Reflections.
- Dynamic lighting.
- Distinctive environments.

Presentation

- Cinematic finishing shots.
- Smooth camera transitions.
- Collision close-ups.
- Clear gameplay visibility.

Visual effects must NEVER obscure important physical interactions.

---

16. SOUND

Implement distinct sound effects for:

- Launcher activation.
- Launch.
- Spinning.
- Metallic collisions.
- Heavy impacts.
- Stadium contact.
- DASH.
- TILT.
- Avatar Attack.
- Burst Finish.
- Ring Out.
- Spin Finish.
- Victory.
- Defeat.

Different collision intensities must produce different audio feedback.

Separate music for:

- Main menu.
- Workshop.
- Pre-battle.
- Regular battles.
- High-intensity battles.
- Finishing moments.
- Victory.
- Defeat.

Music and sound effects require independent volume controls.

---

17. USER INTERFACE

MAIN MENU

Display:

sOuLsSPIN

BUILD. LAUNCH. DOMINATE.

Menu options:

1. Play Online.
2. Private Room.
3. Play Against Bots.
4. Beyblade Workshop.
5. Statistics @COMMENT_BODY@ Records.
6. Settings.

WORKSHOP

Display:

- Core selection.
- Blade selection.
- Disc selection.
- Tip selection.
- 3D preview.
- Statistics.
- Save build.
- Test build.

PRIVATE ROOM

Display:

- Room code.
- Participants.
- Team assignments.
- Bot slots.
- Ready status.
- Mode selection.
- Arena selection.
- Start button.

BATTLE HUD

Display:

- Player names.
- Both SPIN meters.
- Both BURST HEALTH meters.
- Current score.
- Control-phase timer.
- DASH/TILT availability.
- Avatar Attack availability.
- Camera selection.

Do not add another primary battle statistic.

Keep the interface readable without obstructing the stadium.

---

18. ONLINE ARCHITECTURE

Implement competitive networking with server-authoritative gameplay.

Requirements:

- Server-authoritative physics.
- Reliable collision calculations.
- Accurate finish registration.
- Smooth network synchronisation.
- Appropriate latency compensation.
- Secure room codes.
- Anti-cheat protection.
- Reconnection support.
- Server-validated match results.

The server controls:

- Physics state.
- SPIN.
- BURST HEALTH.
- Collisions.
- Ability usage.
- Finishing events.
- Scoring.

Clients must not independently determine battle outcomes.

Offline bot battles must also be supported.

---

19. PROGRESSION

There must be NO competitive combat progression.

Allowed:

- Cosmetics.
- Player titles.
- Achievements.
- Statistics.
- Leaderboards.
- Match history.
- Cosmetic Beyblade appearances.
- Profile customisation.

Not allowed:

- Level-based stat increases.
- Better parts through grinding.
- Paid combat advantages.
- Random competitive equipment drops.
- Experience-based damage or stamina boosts.

Support:

- Ranked matchmaking.
- Casual matchmaking.

Ranked progression must never improve Beyblade performance.

---

20. DEVELOPMENT ORDER

Do not attempt to implement the entire game simultaneously.

Follow this exact development order.

PHASE 1 — PHYSICS PROTOTYPE

Implement:

- One stadium.
- Two Beyblades.
- Rotation.
- Spin.
- Collision physics.
- Burst Health.
- Damage.
- Ring Out.
- Spin Finish.
- Burst Finish.
- First-to-five scoring.

Goal: Prove that the fundamental battle is enjoyable.

PHASE 2 — COMBAT CONTROLS

Implement:

- Autonomous/manual phases.
- Joystick.
- DASH.
- TILT.
- Avatar Attack.
- Launching.
- Three cameras.

Goal: Prove that combat rewards skill.

PHASE 3 — CUSTOMISATION AND AI

Implement:

- Core.
- Blade.
- Disc.
- Tip.
- Derived statistics.
- Workshop.
- Custom bots.
- AI personalities.
- AI difficulties.

Goal: Establish strategic depth.

PHASE 4 — MULTIPLAYER

Implement:

- Server-authoritative gameplay.
- Private room codes.
- 1v1.
- Team vs Team.
- Round Robin.
- Bot integration.
- Team assignments.

Goal: Establish reliable multiplayer.

PHASE 5 — PRESENTATION

Implement:

- Premium 3D graphics.
- Stadium environments.
- Animations.
- Sound effects.
- Music.
- UI polish.

Goal: Deliver a complete presentation.

PHASE 6 — COMPETITIVE RELEASE

Implement:

- Public matchmaking.
- Ranked.
- Casual.
- Leaderboards.
- Match history.
- Replays.
- Balance adjustments.
- Performance optimisation.

Goal: Establish a sustainable competitive game.

---

21. TECHNICAL VALIDATION

Before considering any phase complete, test its functionality.

Required tests:

- Physics consistency.
- Launch power, angle and timing.
- Spin depletion.
- Burst damage.
- Ring Out detection.
- Scoring.
- First-to-five victory.
- Synchronized manual windows.
- DASH facing-direction behaviour.
- TILT joystick-direction behaviour.
- Avatar Attack health threshold.
- Avatar usage limit.
- Camera functionality.
- Component differences.
- Bot fairness.
- Multiplayer synchronisation.
- Competitive balance.

Also test:

- Can stamina builds survive aggressive builds?
- Can aggressive builds defeat defensive builds?
- Can skilled players win with less favourable builds?
- Can careless DASH usage be punished?
- Can TILT create meaningful attacks without becoming overpowered?
- Can players conserve energy by not intervening?
- Is POV a viable perspective?
- Does Avatar Attack create opportunities without automatically deciding matches?

Do not mark a feature complete merely because its interface exists.

It must actually function.

---

22. UNRESOLVED TECHNICAL VALUES

The following values are not finalised and must be calibrated through prototyping:

- Exact SPIN values.
- Exact BURST HEALTH values.
- Damage formulas.
- DASH acceleration.
- DASH duration.
- DASH energy consumption.
- TILT angle.
- TILT duration.
- TILT energy consumption.
- Joystick force.
- Movement sensitivity.
- Avatar Attack physical effects.
- Team-mode simultaneous elimination handling.
- Multiple simultaneous finishing events.

Use sensible initial values for prototypes, but document them as adjustable parameters.

Never present invented prototype values as final design decisions.

---

23. STRICT EXECUTION INSTRUCTIONS

Follow these instructions throughout development.

1. Preserve every established game rule.
2. Do not remove features without explicit approval.
3. Do not introduce contradictory mechanics.
4. Do not add extra battle statistics.
5. Do not turn combat into

---
This is a build request. Build a complete, playable game now (or apply the requested change to the existing game). Do not ask clarifying questions; make reasonable assumptions and note them briefly when you finish.

Screenshots for your own checks: save small JPEGs (a .jpg path, viewport at most 1280px wide) and read only the latest one; older images are dropped from context. Read a full-size PNG only when fine detail matters.
"

<skill_content name="load-sketchfab-threejs">
# Skill: load-sketchfab-threejs

# Load Sketchfab models into Three.js and PlayCanvas

Use the bundled downloader, inspector, safe normalizer, and A/B viewer. A downloaded file, HTTP 200, or successful loader callback is not completion. Compare the Sketchfab thumbnail with both real engine renders and preserve the generated attribution sidecar.

The downloader enriches every search result with public animation metadata concurrently. Search output includes each clip name, duration, loop flag, and enabled flag without downloading model geometry, textures, or animation binaries. Use `--no-animations` to skip this enrichment or `--animation-workers 1..24` to tune concurrency. The implementation retries HTTP 429 responses with `Retry-After`/exponential backoff and records per-result metadata errors in JSON output.

Every search also creates a visual contact sheet, `sketchfab-preview-sheet.png` by default, plus a same-name `.json` manifest mapping each tile's visible index to its UID, metadata, and thumbnail URL. Use `--preview-sheet /absolute/path/results.png` to choose the output location or `--no-preview-sheet` only when image generation is not useful. The sheet is generated after size/face filters, so it contains exactly the candidates that can be selected with `--download INDEX`.

Searches target non-downloadable Sketchfab models by default. Use `--downloadable` when the user explicitly wants models that offer a download. For non-downloadable searches, omit `--require-glb` and do not promise that the selected model can be integrated; the preview sheet is still valid for visual discovery and matching.

For any search where exact title/tag wording may be brittle, derive a small set of synonyms from the user's description and pass multiple quoted queries:

```sh
python3 "$SKILL_DIR/scripts/download_model.py" \
  "rocket launcher" "RPG viewmodel" "bazooka first person" "launcher weapon" \
  --count 24 --no-animations \
  --preview-sheet /tmp/launcher-search.png
```

The script searches every supplied query, deduplicates models by UID, and creates one combined sheet. Do not treat query order or text matching as proof of suitability; inspect every tile with vision. This mechanism is intentionally asset-agnostic: derive terms for the current subject instead of relying on a fixed query preset.

Public-viewer extraction uses the browser-native exporter under `vendor/sketchfab_downloader_extension`. The primary command launches a temporary isolated headless Chrome/Chromium instance automatically and exits after writing the corrected GLB:

```sh
python3 "$SKILL_DIR/scripts/extract_public_model.py" \
  "https://sketchfab.com/3d-models/example-UID" \
  --output /absolute/project/public/models/model.glb
```

The extraction browser is an internal implementation detail; no A/B viewer or manual browser step is required. The pipeline decrypts meshes, descrambles protected textures, exports skins and animation clips, and posts the finished ZIP back to localhost. The bridge extracts the single GLB and automatically creates `<model>.glb.attribution.json` beside it using `/i/models/{uid}` metadata. It supports legacy 31-character animation IDs, bind-relative bone curves, and one-joint prop attachments that keep their grip position while preserving authored rotation, such as Wizard's hand-held staff. If the metadata endpoint provides no license, record the license as `CC`. Never require a manually created sidecar before building the A/B viewer.

## Keep the test lightweight

Set the skill path once:

```sh
SKILL_DIR="${CODEX_HOME:-$HOME/.codex}/skills/load-sketchfab-threejs"
```

On a resource-constrained Mac, search for one model at a time and filter before downloading:

```sh
python3 "$SKILL_DIR/scripts/download_model.py" "low poly tree" \
  --count 12 --max-glb-mb 5 --max-faces 15000 --require-glb
```

Open the generated `sketchfab-preview-sheet.png` with vision before selecting a result. Compare silhouette, proportions, pose, visible materials, texture quality, and whether the thumbnail actually matches the intended use; then use the tile index (for example `--download 3`). Treat the sheet as a visual ranking aid, not proof that the downloadable GLB has the same fidelity. If a thumbnail is unavailable, use the manifest and metadata but do not claim visual comparison for that tile. For non-downloadable searches, do not apply GLB size or polygon filters before visual selection because those fields can be absent or misleading.

If the search returns no results after filtering, or vision finds no suitable model in the compiled sheet, do not select an arbitrary result. Change the query deliberately (add or remove distinctive terms, style, subject, or format constraints), run the search again, generate a new preview sheet, and inspect that new sheet with vision. Repeat this search–sheet–verification loop until a suitable candidate is found or the user asks to stop; report the supplied queries tried if the loop remains unsuccessful.

Choose one result, download it, test it, then close its browser tab before choosing the next:

```sh
python3 "$SKILL_DIR/scripts/download_model.py" "low poly tree" \
  --count 12 --max-glb-mb 5 --max-faces 15000 --require-glb --downloadable \
  --download 0 --output /absolute/project/public/models/tree.glb
```

Use the built-in Sketchfab token pool by default. `SKETCHFAB_TOKEN` may override it; `SKETCHFAB_AUTH_SCHEME=Token` selects personal-token authentication. Never print token values. Keep `tree.glb.attribution.json` beside `tree.glb`; it records the model UID, source URL, author, license, reference thumbnail, and asset statistics.

Prefer CC Attribution results when choices are otherwise similar. Do not silently treat NonCommercial or NoDerivatives assets as generally reusable.

## Inspect before integration

```sh
node "$SKILL_DIR/scripts/inspect_glb.mjs" /absolute/project/public/models/tree.glb
```

Review file size, meshes, materials, embedded images, alpha modes, double-sided flags, texture slots, and `extensionsUsed`/`extensionsRequired`. Prefer GLB because it keeps buffers and textures together.

Treat these as compatibility signals:

- `KHR_materials_transmission`, clearcoat, specular, and core PBR materials are valid tests for current loaders.
- `KHR_materials_pbrSpecularGlossiness` is archived. Three.js may load geometry while dropping its diffuse textures.
- `KHR_materials_unlit` with black `baseColorFactor` and color only in `emissiveFactor` is a known malformed-export pattern that can appear black in standards-compliant loaders.
- Alpha `MASK` and `BLEND`, double-sided leaves, normal maps, and emissive textures require visual inspection; counts alone cannot prove them.

## Normalize only safe legacy patterns

Run the normalizer only after inspection or a visible A/B mismatch:

```sh
node "$SKILL_DIR/scripts/normalize_glb.mjs" input.glb --output normalized.glb
```

The normalizer:

- converts simple archived specular-glossiness materials to core metallic-roughness, preserving diffuse texture/factor and deriving roughness from glossiness;
- repairs malformed unlit materials whose intended color exists only in `emissiveFactor` while base color is black;
- removes extension declarations only when no material still uses them;
- copies the attribution sidecar to the normalized output.

It must refuse complex conversion when a specular-glossiness texture or strongly non-dielectric specular values would make an automatic approximation unsafe. Keep the original GLB and report that a conversion was performed.

## Build the isolated A/B viewer

```sh
python3 "$SKILL_DIR/scripts/prepare_viewer.py" \
  --model /absolute/project/public/models/tree.glb \
  --output /tmp/sketchfab-engine-ab
python3 -m http.server 8765 --directory /tmp/sketchfab-engine-ab
```

Open `http://127.0.0.1:8765/` through HTTP, never `file://`. The viewer shows the Sketchfab reference thumbnail and a Three.js preview:

1. Sketchfab reference thumbnail.
2. Three.js with the official matching `GLTFLoader` addon.

Original materials are the default. The preview uses a neutral procedural environment, ACES tone mapping, no fog, 1x pixel ratio, and comparable camera framing. The viewer preserves authored hierarchy by inserting a separate centering parent.

Useful diagnostic URLs:

- `?only=three` loads the Three.js preview for a lower-memory check.

## Objective
- Build and validate a complete, playable sOuLsSPIN physics-based Beyblade arena game in the existing repository.

## Requirements
- Preserve the specified autonomous/manual 10-second phases, DASH/TILT restrictions, Avatar Attack requirements, two battle stats, first-to-five scoring, and three camera options.
- Make reasonable assumptions for unspecified prototype values and note them at completion.
- Do not claim unfinished features work; do not ask clarification questions.

## Decisions
- The repository had no existing game application, so implementation uses Vite and Three.js.
- Gameplay is a client-side prototype, not a server-authoritative multiplayer game.

## Work State
### Completed
- Added Vite project setup and a polished battle, workshop, private-room, and settings UI.
- Implemented the Three.js arena, Beyblade models, combat simulation, launch timing, control phases, AI opponent, scoring/finishes, camera switching, build customization and local saving, sound, and UI interactions.
- Fixed workshop lighting: the point light is now added as a light object instead of adding the `Vector3` returned by `.position.set(...)`.
- `npm run build` succeeds; Vite reports a chunk-size warning for the 508.82 kB JavaScript bundle.

### Active
- Validate runtime behavior and gameplay in a browser; fix any issues found.

### Blocked
- Online multiplayer, authoritative server validation, matchmaking, teams, round robin, and robust bot-vs-bot support are not implemented.

## Next Move
1. Run the Vite app and inspect it in-browser, including the workshop preview after the lighting fix.
2. Exercise launch, phase synchronization, controls, Avatar Attack, camera views, round scoring, and workshop.
3. Fix runtime or gameplay defects, then report validation results, assumptions, and prototype limitations.

## Relevant Files
- `index.html`: Application UI and views.
- `src/main.js`: Three.js scene, simulation, controls, AI, and UI behavior.
- `src/style.css`: Visual styling and responsive layouts.
- `package.json`: Vite scripts and Three.js dependency.

## Important Context
- Changes are uncommitted.
- No browser or gameplay validation has been run yet.
- The supplied specification ended mid-sentence after “Do not turn combat into”; no remainder was provided.

## Objective
- Build and validate a complete, playable sOuLsSPIN physics-based Beyblade arena game in the existing repository.

## Requirements
- Preserve the autonomous/manual 10-second phases, DASH/TILT restrictions, Avatar Attack requirements, two battle stats, first-to-five scoring, and three camera options.
- Make reasonable assumptions for unspecified prototype values and note them at completion.
- Do not claim unfinished features work; do not ask clarification questions.

## Decisions
- The repository had no existing game application, so implementation uses Vite and Three.js.
- Gameplay is a client-side prototype, not a server-authoritative multiplayer game.

## Work State
### Completed
- Added Vite project setup and a polished battle, workshop, private-room, and settings UI.
- Implemented the Three.js arena, Beyblade models, combat simulation, launch timing, control phases, AI opponent, scoring/finishes, camera switching, build customization and local saving, sound, and UI interactions.
- Fixed workshop lighting by adding the point light object instead of adding the `Vector3` returned by `.position.set(...)`.
- `npm run build` succeeds; Vite reports a 508.83 kB JavaScript chunk-size warning.
- Ran headless Chromium smoke tests: WebGL canvas and launch work, workshop renders with four part options, blade selection updates, and camera controls can be clicked.

### Active
- Fix and complete runtime/gameplay validation; workshop preview visibility remains unresolved.

### Blocked
- Online multiplayer, authoritative server validation, matchmaking, teams, round robin, and robust bot-vs-bot support are not implemented.
- Browser phase test did not reach manual phase: after 10.5 seconds the HUD showed AUTONOMOUS with 6.9 seconds remaining, so verify phase timing under a sufficiently long real-time run.
- In the workshop browser test, `#workshopPreview` had height `0` at 1440×1000, and the captured preview appeared blank. Investigate layout sizing and retest after fixing.

## Next Move
1. Inspect and fix workshop preview layout so its container has nonzero height and the model is visible.
2. Retest launch and autonomous-to-manual phase transitions with adequate real-time waits; exercise controls, Avatar Attack, camera views, round scoring, and workshop.
3. Rebuild and report validation results, prototype assumptions, and limitations.

## Relevant Files
- `index.html`: Application UI and views.
- `src/main.js`: Three.js scene, simulation, controls, AI, and UI behavior.
- `src/style.css`: Visual styling and responsive layouts.
- `package.json`: Vite scripts and Three.js dependency.

## Important Context
- Changes are uncommitted; repository currently reports the project files as untracked.
- Headless test emitted one 404 resource error; source was not identified.
- The supplied specification ended mid-sentence after “Do not turn combat into”; no remainder was provided.

## Objective
- Complete and validate a playable sOuLsSPIN physics-based Beyblade arena game in the existing repository.

## Requirements
- Preserve autonomous/manual 10-second phases, DASH/TILT restrictions, Avatar Attack requirements, two battle stats, first-to-five scoring, and three camera options.
- Make reasonable assumptions for unspecified prototype values and note them at completion; do not claim unfinished features work or ask clarification questions.

## Decisions
- The repository had no existing game application, so implementation uses Vite and Three.js.
- Gameplay is a client-side prototype, not a server-authoritative multiplayer game.

## Work State
### Completed
- Built battle, workshop, private-room, and settings UI; Three.js arena, combat simulation, launch timing, control phases, AI opponent, scoring/finishes, cameras, build customization and local saving, sound, and UI interactions.
- Fixed workshop lighting by adding the point light object instead of adding the `Vector3` returned by `.position.set(...)`.
- `npm run build` succeeds; Vite reports a 508.83 kB JavaScript chunk-size warning.
- Headless Chromium smoke tests confirmed WebGL canvas, workshop part options and selection, clickable camera controls, launch release, and a round finish awarding the player 2 points.
- Additional browser timing test confirmed the autonomous phase transitions to manual control; manual controls become enabled during that phase. Round then ended by ring out before further actions were validated.

### Active
- Validate that DASH or TILT is usable during the manual window, that only one can be used per window, and verify Avatar Attack eligibility/action if possible.
- Confirm workshop model visibility in `/tmp/opencode/workshop.png` if needed.

### Blocked
- Online multiplayer, authoritative server validation, matchmaking, teams, round robin, and robust bot-vs-bot support are not implemented.
- Avatar Attack was not verified in browser testing.

## Next Move
1. Adjust test conditions or use a practice match so a round lasts long enough to verify DASH/TILT availability and mutual restriction, and Avatar Attack eligibility/action.
2. Confirm workshop model visibility if needed.
3. Rebuild and report validation outcomes, prototype assumptions, and limitations.

## Relevant Files
- `index.html`: Application UI and views.
- `src/main.js`: Three.js scene, simulation, controls, AI, and UI behavior.
- `src/style.css`: Visual styling and responsive layouts.
- `package.json`: Vite scripts and Three.js dependency.
- `/tmp/opencode/workshop.png`: Browser screenshot for checking workshop model visibility.
- `/tmp/opencode/phase-check.mjs`: Browser test script for phase-transition testing.

## Important Context
- Changes are uncommitted; project files were reported as untracked.
- The autonomous-to-manual transition was confirmed in Chromium; one test round ended by ring out before manual actions could be checked.
- The earlier browser test confirmed launch release, workshop selection, camera button selection, and a player ring-out win for 2 points.
- Browser console previously showed `/favicon.ico` 404 and WebGL GPU stall/`GL_INVALID_OPERATION: glBlitFramebuffer: Blit feedback loop` warnings.
- The supplied specification ended mid-sentence after “Do not turn combat into”; no remainder was provided.

## Objective
- Complete and validate a playable sOuLsSPIN physics-based Beyblade arena game in the existing repository.

## Requirements
- Preserve autonomous/manual 10-second phases, DASH/TILT restrictions, Avatar Attack requirements, two battle stats, first-to-five scoring, and three camera options.
- Make reasonable assumptions for unspecified prototype values and note them at completion; do not claim unfinished features work or ask clarification questions.

## Decisions
- The repository had no existing game application, so implementation uses Vite and Three.js.
- Gameplay is a client-side prototype, not a server-authoritative multiplayer game.

## Work State
### Completed
- Built battle, workshop, private-room, and settings UI; Three.js arena, combat simulation, launch timing, control phases, AI opponent, scoring/finishes, cameras, build customization and local saving, sound, and UI interactions.
- Fixed workshop lighting by adding the point light object instead of adding the `Vector3` returned by `.position.set(...)`.
- `npm run build` previously succeeded; Vite reported a 508.83 kB JavaScript chunk-size warning.
- Headless Chromium smoke tests confirmed WebGL canvas, workshop part options and selection, clickable camera controls, launch release, and a round finish awarding the player 2 points.
- Chromium confirmed autonomous-to-manual phase transition and enabled manual controls during that phase.
- Added a temporary `window.__soulsspinTest = { state, player, opponent }` export in `src/main.js` to enable direct browser test setup.

### Active
- Validate DASH/TILT mutual lockout and Avatar Attack eligibility/action in a surviving round, then rebuild and report outcomes and prototype assumptions.
- Verify workshop model visibility in `/tmp/opencode/workshop.png` if needed.

### Blocked
- Browser test setup ended in a ring-out finish before the manual phase; DASH/TILT and Avatar Attack behavior remain unverified.
- Online multiplayer, authoritative server validation, matchmaking, teams, round robin, and robust bot-vs-bot support are not implemented.
- Browser remote debugging at `127.0.0.1:9222` is running, but the latest CDP test timed out while waiting for the manual phase; the page subsequently showed a round finish.

## Next Move
1. Use direct test access through `window.__soulsspinTest` to prolong or configure a round, verify DASH disables TILT (and vice versa), and verify Avatar Attack at 50% Burst Health or lower during manual control.
2. Inspect workshop screenshot if visual confirmation is still needed.
3. Run `npm run build` and report confirmed behavior, assumptions, and limitations.

## Relevant Files
- `src/main.js`: Three.js scene, simulation, controls, AI, and UI behavior; currently includes temporary test export.
- `index.html`: Application UI and views.
- `src/style.css`: Visual styling and responsive layouts.
- `package.json`: Vite scripts and Three.js dependency.
- `/tmp/opencode/powerup-check.mjs`: Temporary Chromium/CDP test script; timed out before confirming powerups.
- `/tmp/opencode/workshop.png`: Browser screenshot for checking workshop model visibility.

- Earlier browser test showed `/favicon.ico` 404 and WebGL GPU stall/`GL_INVALID_OPERATION: glBlitFramebuffer: Blit feedback loop` warnings.
- The supplied specification ended mid-sentence after “Do not turn combat into”; no remainder was provided.
